newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Explorer completes historic Antarctic crossing.
newsitem.headline: Explorer completes historic Antarctic crossing.

text.p: Norwegian explorer Borge Ousland became the first person to walk across the Antarctic continent alone and unsupported when he arrived at New Zealand's Scott Base on Saturday.
Ousland arrived at the base, on the Pacific coast of Antarctica, at around 1 p.m. (0000 GMT) after covering about 1,800 miles (2880 km) on foot in just over two months.
He set out from Antarctica's Berkner Island in the Weddell Sea on November 15 last year.
New Zealand's Scott Base operations manager Rex Hendry said the explorer was in good spirits after completing his historic journey.
"He is elated having finished the trip," Hendry told Reuters by phone.
"He's in a very good mood and he looks very physically fit and healthy, although obviously lean. Everything has gone very well for him."
Ousland used skis, a sled and a giant "para-wing" sail to help speed his journey across the world's coldest continent.

One of the most experienced polar explorers, Ousland had already become the first person to reach both of the Earth's poles alone without the aid of dogs, motorised transport or air-dropped provisions.

He reached the North Pole on foot on April 22, 1994, after 52 days alone. On December 21 1995, during his first attempt to cross Antarctica, he completed a trek of 825 miles to the South Pole before frostbite forced him to give up.
Ousland's latest feat marks the first and only unsupported crossing of Antarctica and the longest solo polar trek ever accomplished.
